'''''Eriocapitella''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the buttercup [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Ranunculaceae]]. Plants of the genus are [[Native plant|native]] to [[Asia]].{{r|POWO}} The generic name ''Eriocapitella'' roughly translates to "growing in a small woolly head", which refers to the hairy [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] and [[fruit]] of some members of the genus. Cultivated plants are commonly known as '''fall-blooming anemones'''.{{sfnp|Rudy|2004}}{{r|Herman2004}}

==Taxonomy==
''Eriocapitella'' was named by the [[Japan]]ese [[botany|botanist]] [[Takenoshin Nakai]] in 1941.{{r|IPNI:33128-1}} It was proposed as a [[Section (botany)|section]] of genus ''[[Anemone]]'' in 1991,{{r|IPNI:957630-1}} but later [[Segregate (taxonomy)|segregated]] into genus ''Eriocapitella''.

An artificial [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] is also recognized by POWO:{{r|POWO:77184419-1}}

* [[Eriocapitella × hybrida|''Eriocapitella'' × ''hybrida'']] <small>(L.H.Bailey) Christenh. & Byng</small>
** Basionym: ''Anemone japonica'' var. ''hybrida'' <small>L.H.Bailey</small>
** Synonym: ''Anemone'' × ''hybrida'' <small>Paxton</small>

The parents of the hybrid are ''E. japonica'' and ''E. vitifolia''. Historically, the hybrid was developed in Europe after ''E. japonica'' was brought to England in 1843.{{r|Herman2004}}

===Etymology===
The [[Latin]] word {{Lang|la|capitellatus}} (or {{Lang|la|capitellata}}) means "growing in a small head".{{sfnp|Gledhill|2008|p=90}} Since the prefix ''erio-'' (from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] {{Lang|grc|ἔριον}}) means "woolly" (or "wool"),{{sfnp|Gledhill|2008|p=156}} the generic name ''Eriocapitella'' translates to "growing in a small woolly head". Presumably this refers to the hairy [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] and [[fruit]] of some of the [[Taxon|taxa]] in the genus.

==Distribution==
Plants of genus ''Eriocapitella'' are [[Native plant|native]] to [[Asia]]. They are found throughout the [[Himalayas|Himalaya region]], across much of [[East Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]], ranging as far south as [[Sumatra]].{{r|POWO}}

* [[Western Himalaya]]: [[Afghanistan]], [[Pakistan]], [[India]]
* [[Eastern Himalaya]]: [[Nepal]], [[Assam]] (northeast India), [[Tibet]], [[Qinghai]] (northwest China)
* East and Southeast Asia: [[China]], [[Taiwan]], [[Vietnam]], [[Laos]], [[Myanmar]]
* [[South Asia]]: [[Sri Lanka]]

Plants of the genus have been introduced to Czech Republic, Slovakia, [[Ecuador]], [[Germany]], [[Japan]], [[Korea]], and elsewhere.{{r|POWO}}

==Cultivation==
Plants of genus ''Eriocapitella'' have been cultivated since at least the 17th century, probably as far back as the Chinese [[Tang dynasty]] (618–907). During that time, a form of [[Eriocapitella hupehensis|''E. hupehensis'']] with smaller, semi-double flowers and pink sepals escaped cultivation and spread across China to Japan and Korea. This form of ''E. hupehensis'', brought to England from China by the plant explorer [[Robert Fortune]] in 1843, became known as the '''Japanese anemone''' ([[Eriocapitella japonica|''E. japonica'']]). European [[Horticulture|horticulturists]] crossed the Japanese anemone with [[Eriocapitella vitifolia|''E. vitifolia'']], a wide-ranging Asian species with white sepals. Today there is a large number of '''Japanese anemone hybrids''' ([[Eriocapitella × hybrida|''E.'' × ''hybrida'']]) with single, semi-double, or [[double flower]]s having white, pink, or purple sepals.{{r|Herman2004}}{{sfnp|Rudy|2004}}{{r|Klingaman2006}}

Fall-blooming anemones usually have white or pink blossoms with a globe-shaped seed head. Newly opened blossoms mingle with the seed heads for several weeks between late July and October. The plants thrive in light to partial shade but will tolerate full sun as long as there’s sufficient moisture. Overly wet conditions should be avoided, and mulch should be applied in the fall, especially in northern climates. [[Japanese beetle]]s, black [[blister beetle]]s, and [[foliar nematode]]s can be a problem.{{r|Herman2004}}

At the [[Chicago Botanic Garden]], Rudy experimented with 26 [[cultivar]]s of fall-blooming anemones over a 5-year period beginning in 1998. The experiments evaluated various cultivars of [[Eriocapitella hupehensis|''E. hupehensis'']], [[Eriocapitella × hybrida|''E.'' × ''hybrida'']], [[Eriocapitella japonica|''E. japonica'']], and [[Eriocapitella tomentosa|''E. tomentosa'']]. About 40% of the cultivars had a bloom length of 50 days or more. The longest bloom length recorded was 65 days.{{sfnp|Rudy|2004}}
